name: Tajikistan
summary: A Persian-speaking mountain country in Central Asia; Soviet until 1991; a civil war followed (1992–97).

location.value: Central Asia; about 143,000 km²; over 90% mountains.

terrain.value: Mostly high mountains: the Pamirs in the east, with Ismoil Somoni Peak (7,495 m), and the Turkestan and Zarafshan ranges; lowlands in the Fergana Valley and south-west.

climate.value: Continental: hot, dry summers in the valleys and very cold winters in the high Pamirs, whose snow and glaciers feed the rivers.

resources.value: Large hydropower potential on rivers such as the Vakhsh, an aluminium smelter, cotton, and gold, silver and antimony.

disasters.value: Frequent earthquakes, mudflows, avalanches and floods; Lake Sarez, held back by a natural landslide dam, is watched as a flood risk.

population.value: About 10 million in the mid-2020s and growing fast; most people are Tajiks, with a large Uzbek minority.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural: only about a quarter of people live in towns, chiefly Dushanbe, Khujand, Bokhtar and Kulob.

disease.value: Health care weakened after 1991; problems include child malnutrition, tuberculosis and typhoid outbreaks, as in the late 1990s.

migration.value: Hundreds of thousands of workers, mostly young men, go to Russia each year; many people also fled during the 1992–97 civil war.

economicBase.value: Remittances (about a third of GDP), aluminium, cotton.

tradeRoutes.value: Mountain roads link it to Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China (via the Kulma Pass) and Afghanistan (via a bridge over the Panj River, 2007).

wealth.value: The poorest of the former Soviet republics, heavily reliant on money sent home by workers abroad.

moneyAndTax.value: The somoni, introduced in 2000 and named after the Samanid ruler Ismail Samani, replaced the Tajik rouble.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic in which power is concentrated in the presidency; opposition parties have been banned or tightly restricted.

keyRulers.value: Rahmon Nabiyev, the first president (1991–92), was forced out during the civil war; the current president has led the country since November 1992.

succession.value: The same president has held power since 1992, re-elected in votes criticised by observers; 2016 constitutional changes lifted term limits for him.

institutions.value: A strong presidency, a two-chamber Supreme Assembly (Majlisi Oli) and courts, under the constitution of 1994.

stability.value: Civil war (1992–97) between the government and the United Tajik Opposition killed tens of thousands; a peace accord was signed in June 1997.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small national army; Russia’s 201st Military Base, its largest abroad, is stationed in Dushanbe and Bokhtar.

majorWars.value: Tajik Civil War (1992–97), fought between government forces and the United Tajik Opposition, ending with the 1997 peace accord.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1991; a long border dispute with Kyrgyzstan led to deadly clashes in 2021 and 2022 before a border treaty in 2025.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of the Russian-led CSTO and of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation; China is a major lender and investor.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Inherited Soviet-era schools and high literacy; universities include the Tajik National University, with the Academy of Sciences in Dushanbe.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Mountain roads, including the Pamir Highway, and tunnels such as Anzob linking Dushanbe and Khujand; a few short railways and airports.

religion.value: Mostly Sunni Muslim; Ismaili in the Pamirs.

languageWriting.value: Tajik, a form of Persian written in Cyrillic since 1940, is the state language; Russian is widely used, and Pamiri languages are spoken in Badakhshan.

artsArchitecture.value: Persian poetry such as that of Rudaki is honoured; Dushanbe has Soviet buildings and new monuments such as a statue of Ismail Samani.

socialStructure.value: Tajiks are the majority, with Uzbek, Kyrgyz and Pamiri communities; family, clan and regional ties matter in jobs and politics.

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in Persian culture and the Samanid dynasty (819–999), promoted as a national symbol since independence.

dailyLife.value: Large families live in courtyard houses or Soviet flats; meals include plov, non (flatbread), qurutob and green tea.

ideasReligions.value: Mostly Sunni Islam of the Hanafi school, with Ismaili Shia Muslims in the Pamirs; the state is secular and closely controls religious life.

colonisation.value: Part of the Russian Empire from the 1800s and the Soviet Union from the 1920s until 1991.

riseSignals.value: Declared independence from the Soviet Union on 9 September 1991.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; the years after the 1997 peace saw steady growth, much of it from money sent home by migrants.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
